short_cite: Herzner et al. 2025 (Austria wood fuels and ashes)
full_citation: Herzner, V., Katzlberger, C., Pfeifer, C., Maringer, F.J. and Weigl-Kuska, M. (2025). Determination of 137Cs and 90Sr in wood fuels and their ashes available in Austria. Radiation Protection Dosimetry 201(13-14), 948-959.
notes: READ via summariser (full text). AGES monitoring 2020-22. Cs-137 Bq/kg: wood fuels 0.327-8.36, mean 2.1; chips (7) <0.19-5.22; log (1, Ukraine) 0.327; pellets (58) 0.46-8.36, mean about 2.15; briquettes (3) 0.49-3.97. Ashes 11.8-867, mean 310: chip ash mean 93-96, log ash 113.7, pellet ash (15) 146-867 mean 390-414, briquette ash 129-704. Sr-90 ash 363-1,200 mean 655. Ash/wood Cs-137 ratio (group means, Table 3): chips 58, logs 348 (n=1), pellets 181, briquettes 144. 26 private-household ash samples plus 1 incinerator ash; no bottom/fly split, no mass balance, no K-40. About 30 kg ash per single-family house per year (approximate, not measured). Text and Table 3 differ slightly on pellet means. Companion dose paper (Health Physics 2025) not used.

short_cite: Stoulos et al. 2014 (Thessaloniki wood-burning Cs-137)
full_citation: Stoulos, S., Ioannidou, A., Vagena, E., Koseoglou, P. and Manolopoulou, M. (2014). Post-Chernobyl 137Cs in the atmosphere of Thessaloniki: a consequence of the financial crisis in Greece. Journal of Environmental Radioactivity 128, 68-74.
notes: READ (full text, 7 pp.; copy hosted at uh.edu, publisher version is Elsevier). Winter 2013 air Cs-137 up to 12 mBq/m3 (unit confirmed in the PDF; the AGRIS record wrongly says uBq), peaks on weekends and holidays, attributed to residential wood burning after an oil-tax rise. Wood Cs-137: oak <0.05-1.3, beech 0.05-11.0, plane 8.2, Serbian pellets 5.2 Bq/kg; K-40 12-37 Bq/kg in wood. Ash: local wood 25-499, Balkan wood 31-64, Serbian pellet ash 174 Bq/kg; K-40 in ash 1,592-7,060. Wood-to-ash enrichment from K-40: fireplaces 77-209, wood stoves 107-118, pellet stove 85. Mass balance (using K-40 enrichment as ash-yield proxy) says 41-79% of the Cs-137 in the wood is unaccounted for in ash (0.8-6.5 Bq per kg wood burned). CAVEAT: the wood and ash samples are NOT paired (several come from other cited studies) and K is itself partly volatile; the authors call the result preliminary. Only domestic-appliance estimate of Cs-137 loss found.

short_cite: Stoulos & Ioannidou 2025 (Greece Cs-137/K-40 ratio)
full_citation: Stoulos, S. and Ioannidou, A. (2025). 137Cs-to-40K ratio and wind resuspension factor monitoring in Greece during the last forty years. Journal of Radioanalytical and Nuclear Chemistry 334(4), 2991-2996 (correction in 335(9), 6293, 2025).
notes: ABSTRACT ONLY read. Air Cs-137/K-40 activity ratio by source: Chernobyl 12:7, Fukushima 1.0, Spanish event 0.6, Chernobyl-zone wildfires 0.18, contaminated wood combustion for heating 0.15; 0.04 in 1995. Supports wood heating as a measurable regional air source in Greece; no emission totals. A correction notice exists (10.1007/s10967-025-10181-4); check which values changed.

short_cite: Cantaluppi et al. 2023 (NE Italy wood biomass and pellets)
full_citation: Cantaluppi, C., Morelli, B., Cavalli, R., Greco, R. and Pradel, N. (2023). Natural and artificial radionuclides in wood biomass used for heating: comparison of North-East Italy and imported wood pellets. RAP Conference Proceedings 2023.
notes: ABSTRACT READ (the PDF URL is too long for the fetch tool; the full text was not read). 27 forest-chip samples (Picea abies, Trento) fresh and as ash from a pellet stove at about 550 C; 65 East-European pellet samples 2010-11; Cs-134 below detection. A Lithuanian pellet batch (June 2009) at about 300 Bq/kg Cs-137 gave ash at about 40,000 Bq/kg after burning (ratio about 130). K-40 and ash concentration factor are measured in the paper but not given in the abstract. Companion thesis (Pradel, Univ. Padua, 2021/22, https://thesis.unipd.it/handle/20.500.12608/42386) has 27 ash and 3 chip results but numbers are not in its abstract.

short_cite: Calabrese et al. 2015 (pellets imported to Italy)
full_citation: Calabrese, M., Quarantotto, M., Cantaluppi, C., Fasson, A. and Bogoni, P. (2015). Quality characteristics and radioactive contamination of wood pellet imported in Italy. Open Journal of Applied Sciences 5(5), 183-190.
notes: ABSTRACT READ. 65 pellet samples at Trieste/Gorizia border crossings Aug 2010-Mar 2012 (over 1,500 t, Eastern Europe and Balkans); most very low Cs-137, a few hot spots above 100 Bq/kg. Gives trade-flow evidence that contaminated fuel crosses borders (activity proxy by country of use is not country of origin).

short_cite: Strzalek et al. 2021 (Poland pine and birch wood Cs-137, K-40)
full_citation: Strzalek, M., Barczak, K., Karwowska, J. and Krolak, E. (2021). Activity of 137Cs and 40K isotopes in pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) and birch (Betula pendula Roth) stands of different ages in a selected area of Eastern Poland. Forests 12(9), 1205 (correction Forests 13(1), 58, 2022: wood unit is Bq/Mg, not Bq/kg).
notes: READ (web text). Sokolow Forest District. Cs-137 in wood 150.3 Bq/Mg (30-yr pine) to 3,696 Bq/Mg (80-yr birch), i.e. 0.15-3.7 Bq/kg; birch above pine, older stands above younger; soil Cs-137 at most about 27 Bq/kg, litter 12.7-99 Bq/kg. Low-deposition central-European anchor. K-40 wood values only in a figure. The original article's units were wrong, so cite the correction.

short_cite: Moere & Hubbard 1998 (SSI 1998:15 Cs-137 biofuel large plants)
full_citation: Moere, H. and Hubbard, L.M. (1998). Stralskyddskonsekvenser fran Cs-137 vid anvandning av biobransle i stora anlaggningar (Radiation protection consequences of Cs-137 from the use of biofuel in large plants). SSI Rapport 1998:15, Statens stralskyddsinstitut.
notes: READ via summariser (Swedish). Tables of Swedish fuel and ash Cs-137: household wood Gavleborg 1997 3-300 Bq/kg (ash 2-20 kBq/kg), Stigsjo 42 Bq/kg (ash 80-100 kBq/kg), pine shoots 200-2,000, chips 0.4-4, pellets 35, logging residue (GROT) 180-700 Bq/kg. District-heating ash all Sweden 1990-91 <2-30 kBq/kg; Hasselbyverket 1997 fly ash 6-9 vs bottom ash 0.4-0.5 kBq/kg (about 12-20 times); Ange fly 15 vs bottom 7; Osterbybruk 8 vs 8 kBq/kg. Ash fraction of fuel 2% GROT, 1% household wood, bark 3-5%, stemwood about 0.5%; implied ash factor 50 (GROT). Fly ash usually higher in Cs-137 because Cs evaporates and condenses on the smallest particles. No percentage partition to flue gas; condensate release scenario assumes 10% (or 0.3%) of fuel Cs-137. Origin of the '10% to flue gas' assumption carried into the household report S0515. Some table layouts garbled in source.

short_cite: Moere 2011 (SSM 2011-3342 contaminated wood-fuel ash inspections)
full_citation: Moere, H. (c. 2011). Samlad stralsakerhetsvardering av tillsyn av verksamheter som hanterar kontaminerad tradbransleaska 2006-2011 (Overall radiation safety assessment of inspections of operations handling contaminated wood-fuel ash 2006-2011). SSM diary no. SSM 2011-3342, Stralsakerhetsmyndigheten.
notes: READ via summariser. Publication year not stated; 2011 taken from the diary number (inspections 2006-2011). Industrial, not household: fly ash at inspected plants about 0.1-13 kBq/kg Cs-137 (75 kBq/kg at a closed plant in 2002), bottom ash mostly <1.5 kBq/kg; ash above 10 kBq/kg must be landfilled, below may go to construction or forest; about 110 facilities affected; releases about 3 GBq/a from each of two large construction sites and up to about 0.1 GBq/a from a landfill. No household ash information. Use for the large-plant fly/bottom contrast and ash-disposal rules only.

short_cite: RIVM 2025-0088 (Cs-137 biomass ash reuse, Netherlands)
full_citation: Dekkers, F., van der Linden, M., de With, G. and Mayer, B. (2025). Hergebruik van radioactieve restmaterialen: afwegingen bij hergebruik van cesium-137 bevattende biomassa-assen. RIVM-rapport 2025-0088, Rijksinstituut voor Volksgezondheid en Milieu.
notes: READ via summariser. Belgian data quoted: fly ash Cs-137 100-500 Bq/kg, bottom ash 5-50 Bq/kg; Belarus-origin pellets up to 700 Bq/kg, other origins well below 100; Greek household ash up to 500 Bq/kg; ash-to-biomass ratio about 70 to over 200; fly ash is roughly 20-80% of total ash by mass depending on furnace and method; soil-to-tree transfer factors 1e-3 to 1e-1 (unit not stated). Dutch clearance 100 Bq/kg Cs-137; above it, ash goes to COVRA storage unless cleared; landfilling is the minimum standard otherwise; reuse routes listed (cement, roads, forestry). No emission fractions. Secondary compilation of other studies.

short_cite: Otreshko et al. 2019 (Ukraine fuel wood contamination)
full_citation: Otreshko, L., Yoshchenko, L., Holyaka, D., Polishchuk, S., Kosarchuk, O., Lazaryev, N. and Hrysyuk, S. (2019). Problem analysis and assessment of the prospects of fuel wood use obtained in the territories of the pollution by Chernobyl accident. Bioresources and Nature Management (Biolohichni resursy i pryrodokorystuvannia) 11(5-6). NUBiP Ukraine.
notes: ABSTRACT READ. Author list from Crossref (first author as listed there; confirm). Soil Cs-137 33-675 Bq/kg (20-100 kBq/m2); firewood Cs-137 <2.0 to 690 +/- 83 Bq/kg, about 98% of samples under the 600 Bq/kg fuel-wood limit (GNPAR-2005), 1.1% over; firewood Sr-90 3-473 Bq/kg (14.7% over 60 Bq/kg); Cs-137/Sr-90 ratio 1.4 +/- 0.6 in hardwoods and 4.8 +/- 2 in conifers; wood with Sr-90 above 100 Bq/kg gives ash of 10 kBq/kg or more, which is radioactive waste under OSPU-2005. Sampling years not given in the abstract.

short_cite: Dvornik et al. 2017 (Belarus forest-fire Cs-137, firewood limit)
full_citation: Dvornik, A.A., Klementeva, E.A. and Dvornik, A.M. (2017). Assessment of 137Cs contamination of combustion products and air pollution during the forest fires in zones of radioactive contamination. Radioprotection 52(1), 29-36.
notes: READ. Belarusian hygienic standard: Cs-137 in firewood must not exceed 740 Bq/kg. Cs-137 in ash 2-3 orders of magnitude above that in the burned material (no values in text); over 90% of forest Cs-137 is in litter. Notes that winter air increases in Gomel may come from wood stoves but 'cannot be estimated authentically' for lack of data. No firewood measurements. Regulatory-limit and context source only.

short_cite: Garbaruk & Uglyanets 2022 (Belarus oak wood and bark, CEZ)
full_citation: Garbaruk, D.K. and Uglyanets, A.V. (2022). Assessment of oak wood and bark contamination by 137Cs in the exclusion zone of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant. Journal of the Belarusian State University. Ecology 2022(4), 33-45.
notes: ABSTRACT READ. Bark 2-3 times more contaminated than wood; standing and lying deadwood 25-28% lower than living wood; with the 1,480 Bq/kg standard, oak wood could be harvested in 84% of surveyed stands (72% with bark), and under 740 Bq/kg in 32%. No absolute Bq/kg in the abstract. Published online Nov 2023 per the page; issue year 2022 per Crossref. Belarus regulatory limits 740 and 1,480 Bq/kg.

short_cite: Kashparov 2013 (seminar slides, Ukraine firewood limits)
full_citation: Kashparov, V. (2013). Seminar slides, Ukrainian Institute of Agricultural Radiology, University of Tsukuba seminar, 2 November 2013 (file Dr.KashparovSeminar20131102.pdf).
notes: READ via summariser (slides, partly unclear transcript). Ukrainian limits (Bq/kg Cs-137): firewood for households 600; firewood for technological use 1,500; fencing 1,000; construction timber and pulpwood 1,500; props 3,000. Forest ecosystem components decline slowly, T1/2 20-30 years (citing the Chernobyl Forum 2005); pine-wood transfer varies about 20-fold with site conditions. Firewood collection restricted partly because of ash disposal and fertiliser use. Slide deck, grey; use for limits and the 20-30 y context only.

short_cite: Krasnov et al. 2021 (Polissya pine wood transfer factor 1991-2020)
full_citation: Krasnov, V.P., Orlov, O.O. and Zhukovskyi, O.V. (2021). Dynamics of 137Cs content in tissues and organs of Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) in moist fairly infertile pine type of Polissya of Ukraine after Chornobyl accident. Nuclear Physics and Atomic Energy 22(4), 382-389.
notes: READ (full-text PDF via summariser). One 1-ha plot, three trees felled for tissue analysis, over 100 trees measured. Wood Cs-137 aggregated transfer factor (units 1e-3 m2/kg): 2.3 +/- 0.01 (1991), peak 5.5 (about 2002), 2.7 +/- 0.16 (2020). Deposition 539.6 +/- 65.9 kBq/m2 (1991) and 269.9 +/- 32.0 kBq/m2 (2020). Bq/kg only in a figure. No effective half-life stated; the authors suggest decay contributes to the post-2002 decline. Basis of the derived effective half-life in the notes.

short_cite: Goor & Thiry 2004 (radiocaesium in Belarus pine chronosequence)
full_citation: Goor, F. and Thiry, Y. (2004). Processes, dynamics and modelling of radiocaesium cycling in a chronosequence of Chernobyl-contaminated Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) plantations. Science of the Total Environment 325(1-3), 163-180.
notes: ABSTRACT READ (SCK CEN portal). Three pine stands (17, 37, 57 yr) in SE Belarus; root uptake mobilises 0.53%, 0.32%, 0.31% of the soil pool per year; about half of annual uptake is immobilised in perennial organs. Model: stemwood activity peaks about 15 years after deposition then declines mainly through decay; decay-corrected tree contamination in young stands plateaus about 25 years after deposition. No effective half-life given.

short_cite: Fogh & Andersson 2001 (Bryansk tree rings Cs-137)
full_citation: Fogh, C.L. and Andersson, K.G. (2001). Dynamic behaviour of 137Cs contamination in trees of the Briansk region, Russia. Science of the Total Environment 269(1-3), 105-115.
notes: ABSTRACT READ (DTU Orbit). Seven trees felled 1997, Bryansk: Cs-137 far higher in needles, leaves and twigs than in core wood; no peak in the 1986 ring (deep penetration into the trunk); authors expect continued inward accumulation in core wood. Russia anchor for the qualitative time behaviour; no Bq/kg wood values read.

short_cite: Vetikko & Rantavaara 2002 (understorey spruce Cs-137, Finland)
full_citation: Vetikko, V. and Rantavaara, A. (2002). 137Cs content and distribution in understorey spruces. Radioprotection 37(C1), C1-415 to C1-419.
notes: ABSTRACT READ. Finland 1998 (deposition 24-66 kBq/m2): stemwood is 19-36% of tree dry mass but holds only 4-7% of tree Cs-137; needles 21-48% of mass, 37-60% of Cs-137. Concentrations per unit deposition given for needles (0.098-0.13 m2/kg), not wood. Use to scale whole-tree biomass vs stemwood fuel.

short_cite: Ohashi et al. 2022 (Fukushima decadal wood and bark Cs-137)
full_citation: Ohashi, S., Kuroda, K., Abe, H., Kagawa, A., Komatsu, M., Sugiyama, M., Suzuki, Y., Fujiwara, T. and Takano, T. (2022; author list truncated on source page). Decadal trends in 137Cs concentrations in the bark and wood of trees contaminated by the Fukushima nuclear accident. Scientific Reports 12, 11243.
notes: READ via summariser. Decay-corrected 2011-2020 trends: bark half-lives 2.7-8.7 y (outer bark 3.2-4.9); whole wood 6.8-7.2 y but only in the plots where it decreased (2 of 9); wood concentration INCREASED 2.1-6.4 times in 6 of 9 plots and heartwood rose 2.5-21 times in 7 plots; authors see an approach to steady state in many plots. Japanese firewood guidance 40 Bq/kg. Fukushima, not Chernobyl: use only as evidence that 'physical decay only' is the wrong default for stemwood in the first decade.

short_cite: Hashimoto 2023 (radiocaesium dynamics in forests, review)
full_citation: Hashimoto, S. (2023). Overview of radiocesium dynamics in forests: first decade and future perspectives. In: Agricultural Implications of Fukushima Nuclear Accident (IV), Springer, Singapore, pp. 133-147.
notes: ABSTRACT READ. Wood Cs-137 normalised to total inventory in 2012 mainly 1e-4 to 1e-3 m2/kg (dry weight), i.e. 0.1-1 Bq/kg per kBq/m2; conifer (not pine) and oak transfer similar to Chernobyl values, pine lower (few records); six models project conifer wood normalised Cs-137 decreasing, with uncertainty growing after about a decade. Compilation of Japanese datasets.

short_cite: Amiro et al. 1996 (Cs in biomass fires)
full_citation: Amiro, B.D., Sheppard, S.C., Johnston, F.L., Evenden, W.G. and Harris, D.R. (1996). Burning radionuclide question: what happens to iodine, cesium and chlorine in biomass fires? Science of the Total Environment 187(2), 93-103.
notes: ABSTRACT READ (FRAMES catalogue). Laboratory burns of straw, wood, peat, dulse and radish at 160-1000 C: under typical field-fire conditions 40-70% of the Cs was lost to the atmosphere; the rest stayed in the ash and was soluble. Cs ash enrichment exceeded iodine's. Open-fire, not stove, conditions. The only comparator Stoulos et al. (S0531) cite for their 41-79%.

short_cite: Zhou et al. 2016 (Cs-137 and Sr-90 release on combustion, Chalk River)
full_citation: Zhou, L.J., Rao, R., Corcoran, E. and Kelly, D. (2016). Distribution of radionuclides between atmosphere and ash during combustion of contaminated vegetation. Journal of Environmental Radioactivity 165, 159-167.
notes: ABSTRACT READ (INIS record AECL-CW-11270-CONF-005). Laboratory combustion of Chalk River forest vegetation and organic soil at up to 800 C. Sr-90 release 0.3-0.9% (most stays in ash). Cs-137 release at 800 C: surface litter and twigs 45 +/- 7%, alder twigs 77 +/- 9%, alder leaves 92 +/- 5%, organic soil 2.4 +/- 0.5%; vaporisation dominant; strongly temperature- and fuel-dependent. Direct evidence that high Cs-137 volatilisation is possible at stove-bed temperatures; woody fuel at stove conditions not tested.

short_cite: Yoshida et al. 2016 (combustion of Cs-contaminated forestry waste, Fukushima)
full_citation: Yoshida, H., Ogawa, H., Yokota, K., Arai, S., Igei, S. and Nakamura, R. (2016). Safety decontamination system for combustion of forestry wastes. In: Takahashi, T. (ed.) Radiological Issues for Fukushima's Revitalized Future, Springer, pp. 67-77.
notes: READ via summariser (internal date inconsistency: demonstration test March 2012 in the abstract, March 2014 in the body). Lab: 10 g cedar bark at about 20 kBq/kg: at 300 C about 98% of radiocaesium stays in the residue; 350-450 C 15-25% evaporates; above 500 C about 30-35%. Demonstration burn at 550-700 C: ash 22.2% of raw mass, ash about 440 kBq/kg; 95% of input Cs recovered in collected material; no gaseous Cs detected in the scrubbed exhaust (detection limit 0.2 Bq/kg); about 47% of ash Cs water-soluble. Engineered incinerator with wet scrubber, not a household stove.

short_cite: Holiaka et al. 2026 (Cs-137 release when burning CEZ vegetation)
full_citation: Holiaka, D.M., Levchuk, S.E., Hrechaniuk, M.O., Illienko, V.V., Holiaka, M.A., Protsak, V.P. and Kashparov, V.O. (2026). 137Cs release from combustible materials burning under different environmental conditions in the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone. Nuclear Physics and Atomic Energy 27(1), 70-79.
notes: READ via summariser. Open burning of moss, herbaceous vegetation, litter and green pine branches at six CEZ sites: mean Cs-137 release 0.075-0.45% of fuel activity for dried intact above-ground fuels; green branches up to 24%; higher litter moisture cuts emission about tenfold; Chornobyl wildfires 2020 literature 0.01-0.4%. Open-fire release is far below the lab and domestic estimates (S0531, S0549, S0550); a wildfire/litter analogue, not stove wood. No ash activities.

short_cite: Bourcier et al. 2010 (biomass burning source of atmospheric Cs-137)
full_citation: Bourcier, L., Sellegri, K., Masson, O., Zangrando, R., Barbante, C., Gambaro, A., Pichon, J.-M., Boulon, J. and Laj, P. (2010). Experimental evidence of biomass burning as a source of atmospheric 137Cs, puy de Dome (1465 m a.s.l.), France. Atmospheric Environment 44(19), 2280-2286.
notes: ABSTRACT READ (ASNR record). Two-year series: atmospheric Cs-137 correlates significantly with levoglucosan and non-sea-salt K+ (biomass-burning markers), seasonal dependence. No activities or quantified contribution in the abstract. Qualitative support that regional biomass burning (including heating) is an air source.

short_cite: Carvalho et al. 2011 (vegetation fires, radioactivity in smoke)
full_citation: Carvalho, F.P., Oliveira, J.M. and Malta, M. (2011). Vegetation fires and release of radioactivity into the air. WIT Transactions on Biomedicine and Health 15.
notes: READ via summariser. Portugal, September 2010 fires. Smoke particulate Pb-210 and Po-210 about 100 times the reference aerosol; Po-210/Pb-210 activity ratio in smoke up to 12 (reference 0.30; Lisbon air mean 0.19); U isotopes, Th-230 and Ra-226 about 10 times. Evidence that Po-210 is released from burning vegetation preferentially to Pb-210, but open vegetation fires (litter, shrub), no release fractions, no stove data.

short_cite: Carvalho 2015 (Goldschmidt abstract, biomass burning Po-210)
full_citation: Carvalho, F.P. (2015). Biomass burning and polonium-210 in the atmosphere. Goldschmidt 2015 Abstracts, abstract 475.
notes: READ. Conference abstract: smoke-affected aerosols reach Po-210/Pb-210 activity ratios up to 12, about one order of magnitude above usual aerosol ratios; Po-210 concentrated in particles below 1 micrometre. Supports S0554.

short_cite: Uddin et al. 2023 (Po-210 and Pb-210 in Portuguese trees and fire ash)
full_citation: Uddin, S., Gorgun, A.U., Fowler, S.W., Behbehani, M., Habibi, N., Filizok, I. and Al-Murad, M. (2023). Climate change-mediated atmospheric 210Po and 210Pb distribution: how significant can it be for the inhalation dose to humans? Journal of Environmental Exposure Assessment 2(4), 25 (perspective).
notes: READ. Secondary compilation (Table 1, citing Uddin et al. 2023 for Portugal samples; primary paper not located), Bq/kg dry: trunk wood Pb-210 / Po-210: oak 3.27/5.51; eucalyptus 0.98/1.68; acacia 2.04/4.05; pine 1.43-1.98/0.97-1.53. Bark: eucalyptus 1.88/2.60; pine 2.80/2.87. Leaves 10-20 Pb-210 and 3-49 Po-210. Forest-fire ground ash 402 Pb-210 / 1,115 Po-210; fire-impacted fly-ash aerosol 923-2,070 / 3,604-7,255. Dose figures in the article are not used (D1). Source of the Pb-210 and Po-210 fuelwood range.

short_cite: Dlugosz-Lisiecka & Perka 2020 (Po-210 and Pb-210 emissions, coal analogue)
full_citation: Dlugosz-Lisiecka, M. and Perka, D. (2020). Modeling of 210Pb and 210Po radionuclide emissions from local power plants in central Poland. Environmental Science: Processes & Impacts 22(11), 2291-2297.
notes: READ via summariser. COAL analogue, not biomass. About 50% of the Po-210 and 5% of the Pb-210 in coal were not retained in slag or ash captured by electrofilters (authors' 2017 estimate); fine fractions below 0.58 micrometre carry over 23 kBq/kg Pb-210 and 3.6 kBq/kg Po-210; annual emissions 2017 6.28 GBq Po-210 and 0.59 GBq Pb-210 from two Lodz plants, 171 and 62.8 GBq from Belchatow lignite. Household stoves without electrofilters would retain less. Used only to bracket the unmeasured Pb-210/Po-210 wood-combustion fractions.

short_cite: Haas et al. 1995 (natural radionuclides in spruce tree rings)
full_citation: Haas, G., Schupfner, R. and Mueller, A. (1995). Uptake and long term behavior of naturally occurring radionuclides in tree rings of spruce. Journal of Radioanalytical and Nuclear Chemistry 194(2), 283-289.
notes: ABSTRACT READ (Regensburg repository). One spruce, ring by ring: Pb-210 about 1.7 Bq/kg dry in older rings, lower in younger; Ra-226 about 2.0 Bq/kg, nearly constant; Ra-228 behaves differently (values not in abstract). Single tree, Germany. Not a fuel survey; gives a plausible Pb-210/Ra-226 wood scale consistent with S0556 and S0559.

short_cite: Tasdemir et al. 2026 (natural radionuclides in 15 wood species, Turkey)
full_citation: Tasdemir, T., Cakiroglu, E.O., Dizman, S., Kobya, Y. and Yesilkanat, C.M. (2026). Investigation of radiation dose rates, health risks and radionuclide effects of wood and wood-based materials in indoor areas. Journal of Radioanalytical and Nuclear Chemistry 335(4), 2785-2796.
notes: ABSTRACT READ (via institutional record). 15 solid wood species used in construction, HPGe: Ra-226 1.64-13.26, Th-232 0.76-9.46, K-40 6.08-163.66 Bq/kg. Building timber, not fuel, and Ra-228/Th-228 not reported separately; best available range for Ra-226, Th-232 series and K-40 in wood. Hazard-index results not used.

short_cite: Japan Forestry Agency 2011 (charcoal and firewood Cs indicator values)
full_citation: Forestry Agency of Japan (Rinya-cho), Forest Policy Dept., Management Division and Wood Industry Division (2 November 2011). Notice 23 Rinsei-Kei No. 231: indicator values for radioactive caesium in firewood (40 Bq/kg dry) and charcoal (280 Bq/kg dry). Web page 'shintan1'.
notes: READ via summariser (Japanese). Charcoal indicator 280 Bq/kg (dry), firewood 40 Bq/kg (dry), described as provisional. Gives the derivation basis in S0564. No measured charcoal values.

short_cite: Ojuolape 2014 (tropical wood samples, Nigeria; diploma report)
full_citation: Ojuolape, A.O. (2014). Activity concentration of radionuclides present in some tropical wood samples. National Diploma project report (supervisor A.A. Okusanya), Abraham Adesanya Polytechnic, Ijebu-Igbo, Ogun State, Nigeria.
notes: READ via summariser. Only global-South wood measurement found, and it is NOT FIT FOR USE: student report; sawdust from sawmills, species unstated; abstract and results disagree (K-40 mean 3,120 vs 2,258 Bq/kg; Th-232 160 vs 179; U-238 81 vs 65) and K-40 of 1,800-3,200 Bq/kg is some 10-100 times the 6-164 Bq/kg of S0559 and S0531 (a unit, matrix or ash/dry-basis error is likely). Recorded so the gap is visible, not as a factor source.

short_cite: NCASI TB 0639 (Cs-137 in industrial wood ash)
full_citation: National Council for Air and Stream Improvement (NCASI) (c. 1992). Technical Bulletin No. 0639: Cesium-137 in industrial wood ash: concentrations, fate, and human health risks. NCASI, USA.
notes: NOT READ beyond the catalogue introduction (fetch returned only the intro). Year inferred from bulletin numbering (TB 0634 is dated January 1992) and the Oct 1992 Farber paper it reviews; confirm. Scope per the intro: reviews the Farber residential-ash finding, measures Cs-137 in industrial wood ash and estimates ingestion and boiler-air pathways. Lead for US weapons-fallout-era boiler ash and any measured volatilisation. URL for Steve.

short_cite: FAO Forestry Paper 41 (1983/87, simple technologies for charcoal making)
full_citation: FAO Forestry Department, Mechanical Wood Products Branch (1983, reprinted 1987). Simple technologies for charcoal making. FAO Forestry Paper 41, Rome.

notes: READ via summariser (Japanese). Burning 1 kg of charcoal leaves 30 g of ash and the ash concentration is 28 times that of the charcoal; the charcoal indicator 280 Bq/kg is the ash limit 8,000 Bq/kg divided by 28. In a demonstration, about 90% of the radiocaesium stayed in the ash. Derived here: full retention at 3% ash would be a factor 33, so 28 implies about 84% retention, i.e. 10-16% to flue gas. Charcoal combustion, not carbonisation. Date inferred; page layout garbled.
